title: Review of: "Open-Source Remote Sensing Determination of Carbon Emissions From Tropical Deforestation Scenarios in Southeast Nigeria"
abstract: Ogbodo and colleagues present a timely and policy-relevant assessment of carbon emissions from deforestation in Southeast Nigeria using the open-access Global Forest Watch (GFW) platform.The manuscript's central contribution lies in demonstrating the practical utility of open-source remote sensing tools for subnational forest monitoring in data-constrained environments.In regions where access to commercial very-high-resolution imagery is nancially prohibitive, the use of GFW-derived Landsat-based products for estimating tree cover loss, gains, and associated greenhouse gas uxes is both pragmatic and scalable.The study provides quanti ed estimates of 39.3 kha of tree cover loss , associated emissions averaging ~0.9 Mt CO annually (20 Mt over two decades), and concurrent tree cover gains resulting in a reported net carbon sink.These gures are valuable for informing REDD+ monitoring, reporting, and veri cation (MRV) discussions at subnational levels.A notable strength of the paper is its integration of spatial statistics, descriptive trend analysis, and limited eld validation (DBH measurements of 274 stems) to ground the remote sensing outputs.The emphasis on open-data democratization in forestry science is particularly relevant for developingcountry research contexts and aligns well with global calls for transparent, reproducible environmental monitoring.However, several methodological and interpretative issues warrant clari cation: Emission Accounting Consistency -The manuscript reports both 1.20 Mt CO-eq/year and 909 kt CO/year as average emissions; the distinction between gross emissions, net ux, and removals should be clari ed to avoid confusion.
problem: Subnational forest monitoring in data-constrained environments is often hampered by the financially prohibitive cost of commercial high-resolution imagery, which limits the ability to accurately assess carbon emissions from deforestation and inform policy.
method: This study uses the open-access Global Forest Watch (GFW) platform, integrated with spatial statistics and field validation, to assess carbon emissions from deforestation in Southeast Nigeria, demonstrating the utility of open-source remote sensing tools for subnational forest monitoring in data-constrained environments.
task: The task is to determine carbon emissions from tropical deforestation in Southeast Nigeria using open-source remote sensing data from the Global Forest Watch platform.
innovation: This paper demonstrates the practical utility of open-source remote sensing platforms, like Global Forest Watch, for monitoring subnational deforestation and quantifying associated carbon emissions in data-constrained environments such as Southeast Nigeria.

Carbon Stock Assumptions – It remains unclear whether GFW default biomass-to-carbon conversion factors were used or whether locally calibrated allometric equations informed emission estimates. Field DBH data are described but not explicitly integrated into emission calculations.
